content: Cystic acne, also referred to as nodulocystic acne, represents a severe variant of acne in which the lesions progress into small cyst-like structures. However, these cysts are not true cysts in the pathological sense, as they do not involve abnormal dilations of skin structures. Instead, they are inflamed nodules. While cystic acne is not uncommon, it is less prevalent compared to other forms of acne. The condition arises due to an excessive accumulation of sebum within the pores. Contrary to popular belief, cystic acne is neither caused nor influenced by personal hygiene or the lack thereof. A widely used and effective treatment for cystic acne is isotretinoin, which achieves a cure in approximately 90% of patients. Cystic acne can manifest on various parts of the body, including the face, chest, back, shoulders, and occasionally the upper arms. Similar to more common pimples, these cysts are typically filled with a white, pus-like substance. They are often several centimeters in diameter and can be significantly painful. If left untreated, particularly without the early use of antibiotics in combination with topical creams, cystic acne frequently results in scarring. The severity of scarring varies depending on the individual case. While many scars can be treated, scars on the body tend to respond less effectively to treatment compared to those on the face. In most instances, it is unlikely that all scars can be completely eliminated. After the cysts have largely healed, macules, also known as pseudo scars, may develop. These macules are red patches of skin, sometimes slightly raised, that form in areas where cysts previously existed. They may resemble cysts in appearance. The term pseudo scars is used because, unlike true scars, macules typically resolve within six months and do not result in permanent scarring.
